goes beyond individual cases. For the first time, the researchers developed a comprehensive classification, or nosology, of genetic skeletal disorders in cattle and sheep. The system brings together 43 previously described disorders associated with 45 genes and groups them into 21 categories according to the type of skeletal abnormality. This framework can make it easier for veterinarians to recognize characteristic patterns of disease and establish more precise differential diagnoses. It also demonstrates the potential of whole-genome sequencing as a diagnostic tool in veterinary clinical genetics. Identifying the genetic cause of a disorder is important not only for understanding why an animal is affected. It can also reveal whether a condition is inherited and identify recessive genetic variants that may have consequences for breeding. Knowing that such variants are present can help breeders avoid highrisk matings and reduce the likelihood of producing affected offspring. The implications reach even further. Clinical genetics provides an important link between diagnosis, understanding disease mechanisms and preventing inherited disorders. At the same time, naturally occurring genetic diseases in livestock can offer valuable insights into how diseases develop and may provide opportunities to establish new spontaneous large-animal models for studying similar diseases in other species including humans.

Project description: For people with Type 1 Diabetes, multiple daily finger pricks to check blood sugar levels are common practice. This project evaluates a novel non-invasive technology developed by Liom Health AG, which uses light and artificial intelligence to measure glucose levels through the skin in real time — without finger pricks. Methodology: In a pilot study with 21 participants, a carefully controlled sequence of blood glucose fluctuations was induced to assess the device’s accuracy. Conventional blood glucose measurements and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems were used in parallel. Results: The device readings showed good agreement with established methods, with most measurements falling within clinically acceptable ranges. No health risks or technical issues were observed. Conclusion: The study indicates that painless glucose monitoring without fingersticks or CGM could be feasible. However, further research is required to improve accuracy and reliability before market readiness. In many cases, the answer remains a mystery. Clinical genetics can help solve that mystery by linking what veterinarians observe in affected animals with the genetic mechanisms behind disease. In an international study, researchers investigated 39 cattle and sheep affected by congenital skeletal disorders. The cases represented 19 different disorders and involved veterinary experts and researchers from seven countries. By combining clinical and pathological examinations with whole-genome sequencing, the team identified diseasecausing or likely disease-causing genetic variants for a number of disorders, as well as two chromosome abnormalities. Special molecules with aggregation-induced emission, known as AIEgens, are utilized, which emit particularly bright luminescence upon aggregation. Projects ARIaDNA: Assessing the Response of mountain forests to past climate change Impacts using ancient DNA The climate and biodiversity crises are the most pressing environmental challenges of our generation. Long-term records of ecosystem responses to past environmental change are urgently needed to understand how ecosystems respond to ongoing rapid climate change and develop new management strategies. This is particularly important for long-lived organisms, such as trees, that have a life span vastly exceeding the duration of normal research projects. The ARIaDNA project will take a novel research approach that takes advantage of recent revolutions in paleogenetics by combining the analysis of ancient DNA (aDNA) with established paleoecological methods and dynamic vegetation modelling. Specifically, we will analyze ancient plant material preserved at the bottom of lakes in the European Alps that is up to 14’000 years old. By extracting the genetic information within these remains, we can 1) track the post-glacial expansion of forests across the Alps, 2) reconstruct changes in genetic and haplotype diversity in response to demographic changes, and 3) test if trees were able to adapt to rapid climate warming by studying putatively adaptive loci from populations under strong selection. Project GENICA – Rescuing the untapped paleoGENomic information preserved in Ice CAves to disclose long-term genetic variability of mountain vegetation As global temperatures rise, many alpine plant species are being forced to shift their ranges, often leading to population declines and, in some cases, local extinctions. These changes put the genetic diversity of alpine plants in danger, reducing their ability to adapt and survive in a warming world. Understanding how plant populations have responded to past environmental changes is key to forecasting their future resilience. This project investigates long-term ecological and genetic changes in four keystone alpine and subalpine plant species across the Pyrenees, Jura Mountains, Alps, and Carpathians. We will analyze plant macrofossils—such as leaves, needles, and seeds—preserved for up to 5,700 years in mountain ice caves, which provide exceptional conditions for DNA preservation. By extracting ancient DNA and comparing it with genetic data from present-day populations, we will track changes in population size and genetic diversity over millennia. These genetic insights will be integrated with reconstructions of past vegetation and fire dynamics, based on pollen and charcoal analyses.
